cards.text: Friend, Proverbs hands the mic to a new voice: Agur son of Jakeh, and these are his words, the burden he declared to Ithiel. He opens with, 'I am weary, O God, and worn out.' No hello, no good morning, just TIRED, and honestly? Same.
Then Agur sizes himself up: 'Surely I am the most ignorant of men, and I lack the understanding of a man.' Friend, that is the humblest résumé I have EVER read.

cards.question: True or false: Agur says he has learned wisdom and has knowledge of the Holy One.

cards.text: Then Agur fires off some HUGE questions: 'Who has ascended to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in His hands?'

cards.question: Agur keeps going: who has bound up the waters in His cloak and established all the ends of the earth? Who could do all of that?

cards.text: Then Agur asks what His name is, and what the name of His Son is, and finishes with 'surely you know!' For a man who says he lacks understanding, Agur asks REALLY good questions.

cards.question: Agur says he lacks understanding. So what does he say is flawless?
True or false: Agur says God is a shield to those who take refuge in Him.
Since every word of God is flawless, what does Agur warn against?

cards.text: Agur says not to add to His words, lest He rebuke you and prove you a liar. Flawless doesn't need upgrades, friend, and I say that as a stamper who once 'upgraded' a perfect recipe with TRIPLE sprinkles.
Now Agur talks to God. He says he's asking for two things, and adds, 'do not refuse me before I die.'

cards.question: Agur just said every word of God is flawless. What's the first thing he asks God for?

answers.text: To keep lies far from him
To give him a long life

cards.question: True or false: for his second request, Agur asks God to make him rich.

cards.text: Agur asks for neither poverty nor riches, just 'the bread that is my portion.' Not the whole bakery, just his share, and as a guy who OWNS a whole bakery, I'm sitting with that one.

cards.question: Why doesn't Agur want riches?
And if Agur becomes poor, he says he might ___ and profane the name of his God.

cards.text: Agur's prayer is done. Now he turns to how people treat each other, starting with what you say about a servant to his master.

cards.question: True or false: Agur says if you slander a servant to his master, the servant will curse you and you'll bear the guilt.

cards.text: Then Agur starts a list, and every line opens the same way: 'There is a generation.'

cards.question: Agur's first generation curses their ___ and does not bless their mothers.
True or false: Agur says the generation that's pure in their own eyes really is clean.

cards.text: The next generation has haughty eyes and pretentious glances. You know that look: the guy in the fancy car when you pull up next to him with a missing hubcap.

cards.question: Agur says the last generation's teeth are swords and their jaws are knives. Who do they devour?

cards.text: Then Agur says, 'The leech has two daughters: Give and Give.' Friend, that's every subscription I forgot to cancel.

cards.question: Agur lists four things that never say 'Enough!': Sheol, the barren womb, land never satisfied with water, and ___.

cards.text: Then Agur circles back to the eye that mocks a father and scorns obedience to a mother.

cards.question: What does Agur say about the eye that mocks a father and scorns obedience to a mother?

answers.text: May the ravens pluck it out
May it learn from its mistakes
May it be forgiven in time

cards.text: Ravens AND vultures, friend. Agur does NOT play about Mom and Dad. Next, the man who said he lacks understanding lists four things he cannot understand, starting with an eagle in the sky and a snake on a rock.

cards.question: Agur can't understand the way of an eagle in the sky or a snake on a rock. What's the third thing on his list?

answers.text: The way of a ship at sea
The way of a star at night
The way of the wind in the trees

cards.text: The fourth is the way of a man with a maiden. Then Agur describes the way of an adulteress: she eats and wipes her mouth.

cards.question: The adulteress eats and wipes her mouth. What does she say afterward?

answers.text: I am sorry for what I did

cards.text: Agur's got more threes and fours for us. Under three things, he says, the earth trembles, and under four it cannot bear up.
First on the list: a servant who becomes king, and a fool who is filled with food. That second one is me after I 'taste-test' an ENTIRE batch.

cards.question: Agur's list also has an unloved woman who marries. What's the last thing the earth can't bear up under?

answers.text: A maidservant who takes her mistress's place
A mistress who serves her own maidservant
A son who takes his father's land

cards.text: Then Agur flips it: 'Four things on earth are small, yet they are exceedingly wise.' FINALLY, a list for little guys like me.

cards.question: First on the small but wise list: the ants. They're creatures of little strength, so what do they do that's wise?

answers.text: Store up their food in summer

cards.text: Next, the rock badgers. Agur says they're creatures of little power, and friend, I RELATE.

cards.question: The rock badgers don't have much power. So where do they make their homes?
True or false: the locusts have no king, so they scatter in every direction.
Agur says the lizard can be caught in one's hands. But where is it found?

cards.text: A lizard in the PALACE, and I spent YEARS in a junk drawer. Then Agur's last list: three things stately in their stride, four impressive in their walk.

cards.question: True or false: Agur says the lion, mighty among beasts, retreats when danger comes.
Agur names a lion, a strutting rooster, a he-goat, and a ___ with his army around him.

cards.text: Put me on that list, friend. You should see my strut when I carry a fresh batch out of the oven.

cards.question: Agur says if you've foolishly exalted yourself or plotted evil, what should you do?

answers.text: Put your hand over your mouth

cards.text: In other words, stop talking. Friend, I needed that verse BEFORE I hit Reply All.
Then Agur gives the reason with pictures: churning milk yields butter, and twisting the nose draws blood.

cards.question: So the stirring of anger brings forth ___.

cards.text: Keep stirring, and something's coming out, every single time. And that's where the words of Agur end, friend.

findings.problem: The opening card runs four sentences: '...declared to Ithiel.' / 'He opens with, ...worn out.' / 'No hello, no good morning, just TIRED, and honestly?' / 'Same.'

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences.

findings.problem: The setup 'Agur says he lacks understanding' rules out the wrong answer 'His own understanding.' The word 'So' also links verse 2's confession to verse 5 as cause and effect, which the text never states.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: 'So what does he say is flawless?' presents verse 5 as a result of Agur's lack of understanding. The text leaves the connection between the two open.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: Verse 10 says 'or he will curse you.' The card decides that 'he' is the servant, but the text leaves open whether the servant or the master curses.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The baker has to guess the last item of a list in a poem (fire, wind or the sea). Nothing before the card lets them reason it out, so this tests wording they haven't seen.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: The right answer sounds like the Bible ('May the ravens pluck it out'). The wrong answers sound modern and soft ('May it learn from its mistakes', 'May it be forgiven in time'), so the right answer stands out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: The card asks for the third item in Agur's list of things he cannot understand (ship at sea, star at night or wind in the trees). The earlier cards give nothing to reason from, so it comes down to guessing the wording.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: This story card is only a joke ('Put me on that list... my strut'). It tells no part of the passage and doesn't move the baker forward, yet it cites Proverbs 30:31.

rule.text: Every story card tells part of the passage. Jokes ride along on those cards.

findings.problem: 'In other words, stop talking' repeats verse 32, which the baker just answered on card 14, and adds only a joke. It's a recap card.

The question 'So the stirring of anger brings forth ___.' leans on the previous story card through 'So'. It doesn't say who is speaking or give the churning and nose pictures that make the comparison.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what.

findings.problem: 'Keep stirring, and something's coming out' repeats verse 33, which card 17 just covered. It moves nothing forward, and 'every single time' adds a certainty the text doesn't state.
'every single time' stretches verse 33 in Papa Dorin's retelling rather than in a clearly marked joke.

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes.

findings.problem: Two jokes give Papa Dorin a modern life outside his bakery: 'every subscription I forgot to cancel' (stop 2, card 8) and 'BEFORE I hit Reply All' (stop 3, card 15). papa-dorin.md lets his jokes make up small moments 'around his bakery' and lets him use everyday adult life 'for comparisons'. It doesn't say whether he can claim everyday things like subscriptions or email as his own.
findings.question: Can Papa Dorin's self-deprecating jokes say he does everyday modern things himself (subscriptions, Reply All emails), or should those comparisons be about the baker or people in general?
